items.title: Tech outages are fueling a new doomsday economy
items.summary: Recent technology outages have left some worried about AI cyberattacks and the U.S. electricity grid. The doomsday economy is heating up as a result.
items.body: A spate of high-profile technology outages that grounded planes , halted email access and slowed bank transactions have left many people worried about artificial intelligence -driven cyberattacks and the state of the U.S. energy grid. Government officials have dismissed rumors and speculation circulating online that there could be a nefarious culprit for the series of malfunctions. Despite those assurances, consumers like Sabrina Cepeda are readying for a larger-scale technology blackout or other emergency event. In recent days, the Houston resident has purchased propane and lighter fluid for cooking and heating equipment that can be used without electricity. The mother of three also replenished her backup stockpiles of non-perishable foods, hygiene products and allergy medicine in the event that her family is homebound for several days.

items.title: Prediction markets outlook for stocks in 2026 dims amid AI sell-off
items.summary: Odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000, which were once north of 70%, are extremely low on platform Kalshi.
items.body: As stocks continue their tech-driven sell-off , prediction markets traders are seeing a bleaker outlook for the remainder of the year. On platform Kalshi , speculators place just 6% odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000 in 2026. On Oct. 13, those odds were as high as 72%. Contracts ask traders if the S&P 500 will go above various levels in 2026, and they're resolved using data from S&P Dow Jones Indices. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year as investors continued to dump tech stocks, primarily those with exposure to the artificial intelligence build-out. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 fell into correction territory, too. The Stock Trader's Almanac in a Thursday note broadly agreed that the hopes for a December rally are fading, with the caveat that a "Santa rally" could still appear at the end of the year.

items.title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
items.summary: Pressures weighed on US markets, with the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average pushed into correction territory.
items.body: Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down. The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors. Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week. Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high. The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.

items.title: Rejoining EU ‘on the table’ as UK makes deals on trade and young people
items.summary: All options open in future talks, says Ed Miliband, while prime minister hails ‘a good day for Britain and Europe’ The UK rejoining the EU could be on the table in informal discussions between Andy Burnham and European leaders in Brussels, Ed Miliband has said. The foreign…
items.body: The UK rejoining the EU could be on the table in informal discussions between Andy Burnham and European leaders in Brussels, Ed Miliband has said. The foreign secretary said “all options” would be examined in the process, after the prime minister agreed deals on trade and young people with the bloc on Friday. Agreements on food and drink standards, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme were announced after talks this week. Under the plans, 100,000 young Britons will be allowed to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with similar access for Europeans in the UK. Burnham said the agreement would add 0.5% to the UK’s GDP, a £17bn boost to the British economy. Miliband said Burnham would have further “brainstorming” discussions with the EU in the next year about what could happen next.

items.title: Anthropic’s record IPO collides with tech’s worst week on Wall Street since 2020
items.summary: Anthropic held its historic Nasdaq debut a day before Nvidia's stock closed out its longest weekly losing streak since 2008.
items.body: Startup investor Ben Narasin is so jazzed about Anthropic's blockbuster IPO that he's planning a party later this month at his Silicon Valley home. Sake, vodka and Krug Champagne will be served. Each attendee will be given two jars of caviar. "This is a celebration of the most material, significant, and mind-blowingly awesome event that has ever happened in venture capital," Narasin, founding partner of Tenacity Venture Capital, told CNBC in an interview, adding that he didn't even invest in the company. Anthropic raised a record $93.5 billion in its IPO and an additional $26 billion from tech giants that bought at the offer price. The stock gained 17% in its debut on Thursday, lifting Anthropic's market cap to $1.8 trillion and providing a much-needed windfall for Silicon Valley's startup ecosystem.

items.title: Peterson: The Fed's chairman sees an AI revolution coming. Now he has to figure out what it means
items.summary: Kevin Warsh sees AI at a turning point. He faces tough questions on jobs and interest rates.
items.body: Artificial intelligence is about to sweep through the economy. The Federal Reserve is bracing for impact. "We are at a hinge point in the U.S. economy," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said at a conference he convened in San Francisco on Monday. But exactly when and how the economy could turn, and what that means for interest rates and inflation, isn't yet clear. The meeting of Warsh's AI task force saw the new Fed chairman publicly asking the questions Americans will ultimately expect him to answer. He hinted at a few of his private views on whether white-collar workers could soon face massive job losses , but he largely left the speculation to an array of experts he has assembled to advise the Fed. With the technology racing ahead, Warsh won't be able to put off giving his own answers much longer.

items.title: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
items.summary: The UK-EU deal agreed on Friday covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
items.body: Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year. European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people". Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week. Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

items.title: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day of trading
items.summary: The Nasdaq lost trillions in value, with the AI startup’s IPO failing to buoy it as investors question huge sums being poured into AI buildout Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn? As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock…
items.body: As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory. Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal. Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut. Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile.

items.title: How China is using summits to expand its global influence
items.summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping has helped coordinate yet another photo-op of global significance.
items.body: SHENZHEN, China — For a second year in a row, Chinese President Xi Jinping has brought Russian President Vladimir Putin together with another major world leader on mainland Chinese shores. U.S. President Donald Trump had a trilateral meeting with Xi and Putin on Thursday, after the three met the prior evening during a welcome banquet for the Asia-Pacific Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen. It marked the first time they had met together in person. In September 2025, Xi, Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi briefly laughed together for a friendly photo-op alongside an annual meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization in Tianjin, China. The gathering followed easing tensions between Beijing and New Delhi.

items.title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
items.summary: The US president provided little detail on the potential policy, saying others in his team were hearing about it for the first time.
items.body: Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so. "We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time. Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction. Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in. "We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.

items.title: ‘A new record for entertainment’: Grand Theft Auto VI sales hit $3.8bn on first day of release, developer says
items.summary: The announcement from Rockstar Games would mean GTA VI has already earned more than the entire box office run of the highest-grossing film of all time Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79bn in retail sales on its first day , publisher Rockstar Games has announced, calling it the…
items.body: Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79bn in retail sales on its first day , publisher Rockstar Games has announced, calling it the biggest launch for any entertainment product in history. The worldwide figure was based on company estimates through the end of the day Thursday, the day the game launched. Rockstar said also it had sold 32.5m units of the game on prerelease, setting a record across platforms. “We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you,” Sam Houser, Rockstar’s president and founder, said in a statement. The company said the sales set “a new record for entertainment across any medium … becoming the biggest entertainment launch in history.” The figure is nearly five times the roughly $800m that predecessor Grand Theft Auto V attracted during its first 24 hours in 2013 .

items.title: GTA 6 sales hit $3.8bn in a single day - the biggest entertainment launch in history
items.summary: The mammoth figure surpasses every video game launch and single-day film box office record.
items.body: Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6) saw record retail sales in its first full-day of release , hitting $3.8bn (£2.9bn), making it the biggest entertainment launch in history. Take-Two, the parent company of Rockstar Games, said on Friday the figures were based on estimates through end of day on Thursday and marked a record for "entertainment across any medium". It pre-sold 32.5m copies of the game. To compare, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, this year's highest-grossing film so far, made $2.5bn (£1.8bn) over its entire run in cinemas . Internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare said earlier that PS5 downloads in the UK peaked at 8.6 times normal levels around its launch. New Zealand, where GTA 6 was first available, saw a 14.8-fold spike four hours before, suggesting some players switched regions for early access .

items.title: ‘Little room for error’: what a debt-laden cloud computing company says about the AI boom
items.summary: ‘Poster child of AI bubble’ CoreWeave symbolises increasingly risky business model of datacentre buildout The Egyptians had pyramids. The Roman empire had roads. The early 21st-century tech bros have massive buildings full of expensive glass and metal blocks providing the…
items.body: T he Egyptians had pyramids. The Roman empire had roads. The early 21st-century tech bros have massive buildings full of expensive glass and metal blocks providing the substratum for a powerful inhuman intelligence. Building all those datacentres is taking a while, locals everywhere are angry about them and it is unclear whether the inhuman intelligence inside them is actually going to make their backers rich. This could be a problem for the people building those buildings – and therefore everyone else. Almost no company is more exposed to the downsides of the AI boom than CoreWeave, a band of former crypto miners turned datacentre merchants, which has been called the poster child of the AI bubble. The company sells the raw power for AI, known as compute, out of what it says is a network of 52 datacentres around the world, from Texas to Scotland.

items.title: State and federal battle over prediction markets regulation heats up after midterms
items.summary: States, Congress and the CFTC are escalating the fight over prediction market regulation after the midterms.
items.body: The turf war between states and the federal government is intensifying after Democrats secured control of Congress and key governorships on midterm elections night. While it was widely expected Democrats would step up oversight of the emerging, multibillion-dollar industry if they won control of Congress, the actions after the elections have come from primarily Republican-led states. At the same time, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator for prediction markets — has ramped up its oversight of "mention" markets , where traders speculate on what individuals will say during a speech or broadcast. It's a type of event contract the agency has said is susceptible to manipulation. CNBC first reported on Tuesday that the CFTC placed a hold on the certification of markets related to President Donald Trump's words in mid-November.

items.title: Sessions offer advice on rising energy costs
items.summary: A council is urging people to seek support with rising energy costs on heating this winter.
items.body: A charity is offering free advice on energy bills with prices expected to climb further from January . Devon Communities Together said it was hosting drop-in sessions across the county, which include help with energy bills, smart meters and switching suppliers. Gas and electricity bills for a typical household are forecast to rise by £443 a year from January. Heating oil prices have also risen drastically since the start of this year , from about 60p to £1.11 a litre, according to the Action with Communities in Rural England network. Devon County Council said many households in rural parts relied on heating oil because they were not connected to mains gas.

items.title: China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve
items.summary: Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035 Cop31 live – latest updates China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior…
items.body: China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said. Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.” China is the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases by far, producing more than a quarter of the world’s total, so its push for electrification is significant. At Cop31, countries are being asked to sign up to a target of deriving 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035 .

items.title: International first class is over for U.S. airlines. Enter the mega business-class cabin
items.summary: Airlines are opting to build giant business-class cabins with ever-more luxurious suites.
items.body: The era of U.S. airlines' long-haul, international first class ended this week when American Airlines' last flight with its eight-suite section landed. In its place will be a massive business-class cabin with room for 70 passengers. U.S. airlines have been ditching international first-class cabins for a new top tier: larger and souped-up business classes, featuring suites with sliding doors, the design du jour. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines have already taken this step. American was the last of the U.S. airlines to still have first class on long-haul international routes. Many travelers might not notice the difference. That's because of airlines' investments into business class: new suites , bigger screens, better technology like device-charging pads, and improved bedding. It's part of airlines' big bet on mass luxury.

items.body: A spate of prominent departures and years of public battling over its ownership have ensured the Telegraph’s newsroom has been no stranger to internal intrigue and speculation in recent times. Even by its own high standards, however, its offices have been fraught with rumours about its leadership this week. Speculation swirled about the future of both its editor, Chris Evans, and his loyal deputy, Rob Winnett. It was accompanied by days of long, hushed meetings between senior figures at the title, now under the ownership of the German media company Axel Springer . The intrigue was heightened by Evans’s apparent early return from a trip to the US. Suggestions did the rounds that both editor and deputy could be leaving – a rumour dampened by Evans’s continued presence in the newsroom. In the event, it emerged that only Winnett was departing.

items.summary: Campaigners call out ‘greed’ of developers after 95% of ‘megashed’ planning applications approved in last 10 years When a planning application for a lot next to his new home landed in his letterbox, Jon Davis was crestfallen. He had just moved into the property in Bingham,…
items.body: When a planning application for a lot next to his new home landed in his letterbox, Jon Davis was crestfallen. He had just moved into the property in Bingham, Nottinghamshire , with his wife and toddler in June. Now, he said he was being told: “‘By the way, there’s going to be 21.5-metre-high warehouses right next to you, and there’s going to be eight of them, and you’re going to have 400 HGVs and it’s going to be a 24-hour operation’.” That planning application would add to the more than 8,500 warehouses or large distribution units that have been approved across England in the past decade, fuelled by the growth of online shopping. Analysis of official figures by the Guardian showed that almost all (95%) of the 9,009 planning applications for “megasheds” were given the go-ahead in the 10 years up to June 2026.

items.title: Trump vows to stop U.S. companies from building data centers abroad, threatens 'tremendous tax'
items.summary: Trump spoke at the White House after meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a historic trilateral summit in China.
items.body: President Donald Trump on Friday said U.S. companies will be banned from building data centers in other countries and will face a "tremendous tax" penalty if they do so. "We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," Trump said at a White House press conference before announcing the new policy — which apparently came as news to his own staff. "I don't know if that's a breaking story," Trump said. "I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now they're here." Trump's latest push for more data-center construction in the U.S. came despite Americans repeatedly stating — and showing with their votes — that they dislike the structures. CNBC's All-America Economic Survey found that 64% of registered voters opposed an AI data center within 10 miles of their home, while just 13% of respondents said they would support one.

items.summary: Canadians have put a lot of trust in their prime minister but some question if it can last if the trade wars were to end In the hours after polls in the US midterm elections closed and it became clear that Donald Trump had been rebuked in historic fashion, Canadian politicians…
items.body: In the hours after polls in the US midterm elections closed and it became clear that Donald Trump had been rebuked in historic fashion, Canadian politicians were elated. “I was doing cartwheels down the street, and have you ever seen a big guy like me doing cartwheels?” said Ontario premier Doug Ford, a prominent critic of American tariffs. For more than a year, Canada has stared down crippling levies on key industries, threats of annexation and petty feuds on social media launched by the president of the United States. Now, finally, there was a sense within Canada that it could be entering the next stage in its “war” with its ally.

items.title: Tourists are throwing fewer coins into Rome’s Trevi fountain – is €2 entry fee to blame?
items.summary: Charity that collects the coins says donations are down by £200,000 after a barrier was put in place to restrict access When Jeff Clinton, an American visiting Rome with his wife for the first time, found a US one-cent coin on a street close to Termini train station, he knew…
items.body: When Jeff Clinton, an American visiting Rome with his wife for the first time, found a US one-cent coin on a street close to Termini train station, he knew precisely what he was going to do with it. “I’ll throw it into the Trevi fountain,” said Clinton, holding the copper coin in the palm of his hand as the couple admired the landmark. He was well aware of the tradition among tourists of tossing a coin over their shoulder and into the waters of the baroque masterpiece, in a ritual fabled to ensure a return visit to the city or make other dreams come true. But the only thing holding him back from partaking in the gesture was the distance: the steps towards the fountain’s sunken basin are separated by a low barrier and accessible during the day only by Rome’s residents or visitors who pay €2 (£1.64).

items.title: Europe's cyber weak spot is the everyday businesses nobody thought to protect
items.summary: Known vulnerabilities are leaving everyday businesses increasingly exposed to cyber sabotage, as AI enables cybercriminals to work better and faster.
items.body: Cyberattacks on refrigerators in French supermarkets in October spurred Swedish chain Coop to act. But it wasn't fast enough. Attackers hit refrigeration systems in seven of its stores in early November. The affected stores had been scheduled for security upgrades just two days later, a company spokesperson told CNBC. Mundane but essential equipment, used by everyday businesses, has become a favorite target of cyber saboteurs in recent weeks. Experts are warning that a combination of known vulnerabilities, basic security failures and ambiguity over whether suppliers or their clients are responsible are making things worse, as AI makes cyber threats faster and more sophisticated.

items.body: SAO PAULO -- Peru can serve as an entry point into South America for Japanese companies, Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori said, highlighting the country's relatively strong economic growth and improving security situation.

items.title: I hated life as a Neet. But now I’ve found a job, life is just as precarious | Emilija Morrison
items.summary: The government’s plans to help young people not in education, work or training are welcome – I dearly hope they offer long-term security Emilija Morrison is a University of Glasgow graduate and holds a Gold Standard NCTJ Diploma in journalism What child dreams of being…
items.body: W hat child dreams of being unemployed when they grow up? You can probably remember the days, aged 10, when you were asked to present to the class what you wanted to be. Imagine hearing this: “I want to be unemployed. After I graduate from university, I want to go to the jobcentre in my home town and collect my benefits every month.” Yet that is the reality for many young people today – childhood dreams to become a teacher, a doctor, an engineer or whatever other profession thwarted not by the limits of their abilities, but the reality of the economy. One in eight young people aged 16 to 24 in the UK are classed as not in education, employment or training (Neet). Until I finally secured an office job this September I was one of them, going down to the jobcentre every week hoping there’d finally be a good work opportunity.

items.title: An early breakdown in the polar vortex is threatening already depleted gas stocks
items.summary: Colder weather and low wind speeds could strain Europe’s gas market, where storage started winter at its lowest level in more than a decade.
items.body: An unprecedented early breakdown of the stratospheric polar vortex and a record-breaking El Niño event has put energy traders on alert this winter, with analysts warning the weather and climate phenomena could have an outsized impact on Europe. Meteorologists are currently observing a record early breakdown of the polar vortex, a large-scale circulation of strong winds that typically keeps extremely cold air over the North Pole. Changes in the strength and shape of the polar vortex can influence weather patterns much lower down in the atmosphere, potentially bringing in colder weather to parts of Europe and North America. This year, however, the collapse of the stratospheric polar vortex, or SPV, is taking place at the same time as an unusually powerful El Niño, a climate event that can boost global temperatures and disrupt rainfall.

items.title: Chinese 3D printer maker Bambu Lab scales up production in Shenzhen

items.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
items.summary: It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at…
items.body: A ndy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory. Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform.

items.title: Zscaler stock jumps 18% on report that CrowdStrike in talks to buy security vendor
items.summary: Cybersecurity companies have been hunting for acquisitions in the AI era.
items.body: Zscaler shares surged 18% in extended trading on Friday after Bloomberg reported that CrowdStrike is in talks to buy the cybersecurity vendor. Shares of CrowdStrike shares fell more than 8%. The talks between the two companies are ongoing, Bloomberg reported, citing sources familiar in the matter. CrowdStrike declined to comment on the report. Zscaler didn't immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. CrowdStrike has been one of the big cybersecurity winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with its stock about doubling in value this year, lifting its market cap to $235 billion. Zscaler, meanwhile, is down 13% this year, pushing its market cap down to about $32 billion. Along with CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks has seen its business boom as businesses race to upgrade their networks in the AI era. Palo Alto closed Friday at a nearly $282 billion market cap.

items.title: Battery maker GS Yuasa targets defense, space as growth fields: CEO
items.body: KYOTO, Japan -- GS Yuasa aims to grow its lithium-ion battery business for satellites by developing mass production technologies for smaller batteries and automating inspection processes, President and CEO Takashi Abe told Nikkei in an interview.

items.title: I’m a priest. Silicon Valley’s search for the ‘soul’ of AI is deeply troubling | Rev Kevin Deal
items.summary: Humans experience beauty and sit with mysteries. Unlike AI, we do not exist merely for utility Last month, religious leaders from across San Francisco gathered behind closed doors to discuss what it means to be human in the age of artificial intelligence. Anthropic, the AI…
items.body: Last month, religious leaders from across San Francisco gathered behind closed doors to discuss what it means to be human in the age of artificial intelligence. Anthropic, the AI company operating only a couple of miles from my parish, has been courting priests, rabbis and theologians. Its billionaire cofounder, Christopher Olah, has even pressed Vatican advisers to take seriously the possibility that his company’s chatbot might possess consciousness. As a priest, I find this pursuit deeply troubling. I welcome serious conversations about AI’s moral implications, especially theological ones. But the extraordinary effort to establish whether a machine might have consciousness, or possess a soul, reveals a profound misunderstanding of what makes us human. We as humans make mistakes, sometimes catastrophic ones, and then we may or may not try to correct course.

items.title: I never wanted the American Dream and I felt like something was wrong with me—until I moved abroad
items.summary: "I realized it was okay to want something different," says Cepee Tabibian, who moved to Spain in 2015 at age 35.
items.body: I got my first job at 17, working the register at an Eckerd's drugstore in Texas. My manager was only a few years older than me, and while my coworkers seemed motivated by the idea of working their way up to his position, I felt no desire to follow that path. It all felt suffocating: the added responsibility, the longer hours, the idea that this was the ladder I was supposed to want to climb. I wanted to work, but I couldn't wrap my head around building my whole identity around a job. I never wanted the American Dream I saw so many people around me striving to achieve. For a long time, I wondered if something was wrong with me. It wasn't until I finally made a long-term move abroad about a decade ago that I realized it was okay to want something different. After college, I got a job in travel sales. I was good at it.

items.summary: The encroachment of artificial intelligence smells like the death of sport. Can we find the will and collective backbone to resist? There was an interesting development this week in the endless rolling mega-froth over tech billionaire Jensen Huang , a saga that may or may not…
items.body: The encroachment of artificial intelligence smells like the death of sport. Can we find the will and collective backbone to resist? T here was an interesting development this week in the endless rolling mega-froth over tech billionaire Jensen Huang , a saga that may or may not have involved some kind of adulterous 63-year-old honey trap spy dynamic . The latest suggestion being punted about is that, whatever his raw human frailties, Huang is in fact “irreplaceable” as the president of Nvidia. Only this guy can do it. Only this leather-jacketed human visionary, who looks in every available photo like your GCSE chemistry teacher’s profile pic on TerrifiedUkrainianSinglesWantToDateYou.com, can manage this key artificial intelligence mission.

items.title: Trump says he discussed Jensen Huang with Xi; Bessent tells CNBC Nvidia chip export policy is unchanged
items.summary: Trump said he discussed Jensen Huang with China's Xi. Bessent said the ousted Nvidia CEO didn't come up in talks he had while in China.
items.body: President Donald Trump on Friday said he and Chinese leader Xi Jinping discussed their shared affinity for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during their talks in China this week. Earlier in the day, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the ousted leader was not mentioned in separate talks he had with Chinese officials. "I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, 'Oh, brilliant, brilliant! He's a brilliant man.' He is," Trump said at a White House press conference. Asked earlier Friday on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" if Huang, a close ally of Trump 's, had come up in "any of your discussions with the Chinese," Bessent said "no," without elaborating. A senior Trump administration official later said that both Trump's and Bessent's remarks were correct, and that both were addressing their own conversations.

items.summary: Jamie Dimon says he is ‘setting an example’ in seeking to claw back Labour’s increase in surcharge, from 3% to 6% Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said he will find ways to offset the chancellor’s tax rise for banks, calling the increase unfair. Speaking at an…
items.body: Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said he will find ways to offset the chancellor’s tax rise for banks, calling the increase unfair. Speaking at an event in London on Thursday, Dimon said he would seek to claw back the increase and was “setting an example so that [governments] understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”. The bank surcharge is to rise from 3% to 6% in January as a temporary 15-month measure. It was unclear how JP Morgan , which employs 23,000 people in the UK, would make up for the extra cost. In comments first reported by the Financial Times, citing people who attended the event, Dimon said he would set an example in making up for the added costs, and that the decision was “more in sorrow” than in anger.

items.title: Anthropic defied the odds in its record IPO. Now it has to reckon with AI market turbulence
items.summary: Anthropic faced a market sell-off, raging anti-AI sentiment and a crisis at Nvidia in pulling off the largest IPO on record.
items.body: The moment felt impossible. Between Jensen Huang's shocking exit from chip giant Nvidia , voters' rebuke of artificial intelligence in this month's midterm elections, and rising interest rates that threatened to stymie plans for a multitrillion-dollar infrastructure buildout, there seemed to be no way Anthropic could carry out an initial public offering. Anthropic's response? Let's go! "Very few companies would've attempted it in this environment," said Byron Deeter , a partner at Bessemer Venture Partners, which counts Anthropic as its biggest investment ever, in an interview.

items.title: Judge approves $7.25bn Bayer payout to settle claims that Roundup causes cancer
items.summary: German company faced 65,000 claims from people who said they developed cancer after using weedkiller A Missouri judge on Friday approved Bayer ’s $7.25bn settlement of lawsuits ⁠alleging that its weedkiller ​Roundup causes cancer, potentially resolving litigation that has…
items.body: A Missouri judge on Friday approved Bayer ’s $7.25bn settlement of lawsuits ⁠alleging that its weedkiller ​Roundup causes cancer, potentially resolving litigation that has weighed on the German company for close to a decade. Judge Timothy Boyer of a state court in St Louis ⁠found the settlement “fair, reasonable and adequate”. He overruled objections that payouts to individual cancer victims would be too low because claimants who previously settled were paid more. The judge also said delaying payouts could ⁠force victims, including those whose cancer is terminal, to wait “an indeterminate number of years” to be paid. Bayer had faced approximately ​65,000 claims in US state and federal courts from ‌people who said they developed cancer ‌after using Roundup at home or on the job. The settlement announced in February aimed to resolve nearly all current ‌and future Roundup claims in the US.

items.title: Warsh wants Fed officials to talk less. Instead, they’re talking more
items.summary: Fed officials have been rushing to the microphones lately while the Fed chairman stays on the sidelines.
items.body: In his first six months as Federal Reserve chairman, Kevin Warsh has diligently avoided signaling where he sees monetary policy and interest rates headed. His colleagues have been only too happy to fill the void. Fed officials have been rushing to the microphones lately, voicing sometimes conflicting opinions on how the central bank should be handling an inflation bug that the economy can't seem to shake. Most agree that rates should be raised — and soon. Some are willing to hike at a measured pace as conditions play out, while others, such as Governor Christopher Waller and St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem , entertain the thought of more aggressive hikes in a shorter period of time.

items.body: Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan. In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war. Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders. At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.

items.title: Gap names new Athleta CEO, says Old Navy turnaround is seeing signs of progress
items.summary: Gap on Thursday announced Ashley Kechter as the new CEO of Athleta. The retailer also reported mixed fiscal third-quarter earnings.
items.body: Gap Inc. on Thursday announced Ashley Kechter will be the next president and CEO of its Athleta brand, effective Dec. 14. The retailer also said Old Navy's turnaround is showing signs of progress, sending shares up more than 11% Friday. Kechter comes to Gap from activewear retailer Vuori, where she was global president and oversaw the brand's global business strategy, marketing and financials. She was previously global brand president of Fabletics and began her career at Gap before that. "I'm excited to return to Gap Inc. and partner with [Gap CEO Richard Dickson] and the team to strengthen our connection with customers and shape the brand's next chapter," Kechter said in a statement. The announcement comes after Lululemon poached former Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger to be its chief product officer last month.

items.title: UK operation wards off risk of cyber-attack on supermarket fridges and freezers
items.summary: News of vulnerability comes after retailers in at least seven European countries hit by cyber-attacks A secret government cybersecurity operation recently warded off the risk of a cyber-attack on fridges and freezers in UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations…
items.body: A secret government cybersecurity operation recently warded off the risk of a cyber-attack on fridges and freezers in UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums, it has emerged. An attack would have been similar to those that have caused many millions of euros of damage in continental Europe in recent months. But, while many retailers have now been protected, researchers warned that many more could still be vulnerable. News of the operation led by Whitehall and the National Cyber Security Centre, first reported by the BBC, follows a cyberattack this month of supermarket chains in at least seven European countries. Another wave of attacks also affected hundreds of retailers across France in October in an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression” for which Paris has publicly blamed Iran .

items.title: Data center construction costs soar 13% in 2026
items.summary: The demand for large data centers in the U.S. this year, driven by AI needs, grew beyond the supply of powered land and the labor to build these structures.
items.body: A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox. The demand for large-scale data centers in the U.S. this year, driven by the need for computing power for artificial intelligence, grew well beyond the supply of powered land and the labor to build these structures. It also pushed timelines and risk for contractors. All that resulted in costs rising 13% year-over-year to more than twice the global rate, according to a new report from Turner & Townsend, a global project management company. The gain this year was about three times the last ten-year average.

items.title: New York City lawmakers propose ban on restaurants boiling lobsters alive
items.summary: Sponsors cite ‘studies’ indicating crustaceans experience significant pain when boiled alive without being stunned New York City lawmakers are proposing a ban on restaurants boiling lobsters alive. If passed, legislation introduced in the city council, sponsored by Bronx…
items.body: New York City lawmakers are proposing a ban on restaurants boiling lobsters alive. If passed, legislation introduced in the city council, sponsored by Bronx Democrat Oswald Feliz and lower Manhattan’s Harvey Epstein, would ban restaurants from boiling lobsters, crabs and other crustaceans. However, it would not prohibit restaurants from serving lobster or crab prepared by other methods. A first violation would carry no monetary penalty with a second or subsequent violation resulting in a civil penalty of up to $100 per violation, the legislation proposes . The sponsors cited “recent scientific studies” indicating that crustaceans commonly served in restaurants experience significant pain when boiled alive without first being stunned, according to a memo accompanying the legislation.

items.title: Bitcoin sell-off: Crypto is failing the 'digital gold' test again as it sinks with stocks
items.summary: Bitcoin’s sell-off is tracking risk assets again as experts weigh rates, ETF flows, politics and whether the crypto can function as a market hedge.
items.body: Bitcoin 's latest sell-off is reviving doubts that it can behave as the "digital gold" market hedge that crypto backers have long envisioned. Coming into 2026, experts said that showing bitcoin could serve as a market hedge rather than a risk-on asset that moves up and down with growth stocks was an important test for the cryptocurrency. Bitcoin was trading under $62,000 on Friday morning, down from an all-time high of more than $126,000 in early October last year. Its downward spiral in recent months and weeks has been precipitated by a confluence of factors.

items.title: ‘Like an invisible stealth tax’: ways to shield your cash from UK inflation
items.summary: With living costs set to rise higher in 2027, here’s how you can help your savings and pension keep up with soaring prices For many of us, it is when we go to the supermarket that we really notice the impact of inflation. The trolley-load of groceries that used to cost £80 has…
items.body: F or many of us, it is when we go to the supermarket that we really notice the impact of inflation. The trolley-load of groceries that used to cost £80 has broken the £100 barrier , and some of the packets look smaller than they were. But inflation also acts as an invisible stealth tax on savings cash, silently taking a bite out of many people’s nest-eggs. When it is running high, the odds are that your savings are being eroded. UK inflation rose to 3.6% in October and the Bank of England expects it to rise even further, to about 5% by mid-2027 , as higher energy prices continue to push up costs and bills. If your savings account interest rate is lower than the inflation rate, you are losing money in real terms, even if the balance in your account is growing. It is much easier to beat inflation if you do not pay tax on the savings interest you earn.

items.title: Bitcoin's regulation bull case is played out. What could drive crypto gains moving forward
items.summary: Crypto investors are looking beyond Congress for the next catalyst after the Senate failed to advance the Clarity Act in September.
items.body: Crypto investors are hunting for the next positive catalyst after U.S. crypto regulation — a longtime market driver — fizzled in 2026. Bitcoin traded around $61,500 on Friday, a more than 50% decline from its all-time high above $126,000 reached in October 2025. The broader digital asset market has struggled after the Clarity Act, a crypto market structure bill, failed to advance in the Senate in September. Investors now see Wall Street's embrace of blockchain technology — particularly tokenization — as the next trend to give bitcoin a boost. "Every single traditional firm is now looking at digital assets," BitGo CEO Mike Belshe told CNBC last week in an exclusive interview from the fintech-focused Cantor Convergence conference in Miami Beach. That includes BlackRock , the world's largest asset manager.

items.title: ‘The doom of humanity’: will the quest to make robotic hands render us obsolete?
items.summary: The one thing stopping AI taking over the world – or at least everyone’s jobs? Dexterity. Human hands are anatomical marvels that engineers have struggled for years to replicate. Experts are racing to change that Just outside Luton, in an Amazon warehouse the size of four…
items.body: J ust outside Luton, in an Amazon warehouse the size of four football pitches, yellow shelving units pirouette in a digitally choreographed dance. Tubs containing a Lego Spider-Man kit, followed by dishwasher tablets, followed by a pouch of muscle building protein powder whiz along conveyor belts, until they arrive at a human being tasked with stacking the shelving unit that has come to a stop in front of their workstation. This, Amazon says, is the “symphony of people and technology” to which the retail giant owes its success. Following a barrage of negative publicity about working practices, Amazon began to open up its fulfilment centres to carefully controlled free public tours a decade ago. Our guide tells us about the competitive rates of pay Amazon workers receive, their pensions, dental cover and options for flexible working. Her delivery is somewhat robotic.
